# Phase Two — Gevurah Critique: Bound the Repair by Real Ownership

The Awtsmoos gives every ohr a keli and every possibility a border;
Awtsmoos.com must improve the lived road without trampling concurrent work or inventing a new order.

## Known boundaries
- Shared checkout contains unrelated dirty work and active Heichel edits.
- Whole-file rewrites only; no partial patches.
- Touched source uses tabs, full documentation, B"H prologue, Awtsmoos and Awtsmoos.com.
- No touched source file may exceed 120 lines; split responsibilities instead.
- Production deployment requires the repository's real release machinery; Git push alone was insufficient.

## Twenty safeguards
1. Trace the exact template caller that supplies reader server data.
2. Do not rename template variables until call sites are known.
3. Do not swallow reader errors; translate them into bounded user-facing recovery.
4. Keep reader APIs and URL contracts stable.
5. Inspect existing reader tests before adding a new test.
6. Inspect Heichel dirty diff before touching any overlapping file.
7. Prefer a clean worktree for new cross-page changes when overlap is risky.
8. If current Heichel edits are good, preserve them as observed candidate work rather than recreate them.
9. Never stage unrelated repository changes.
10. Keep primary navigation reachable with one thumb.
11. Keep bottom bars below content and include safe-area clearance.
12. Avoid `position: fixed` for large multi-row controls on phones.
13. Allow only compact single-row fixed actions when truly persistent.
14. Do not hide essential publishing validation behind advanced disclosures.
15. Keep form labels and errors visible when fields are active.
16. Preserve keyboard navigation and native details semantics.
17. Preserve reduced-motion and reduced-transparency behavior.
18. Test fallback/loading/error states, not only happy paths.
19. Verify actual production source signatures after deployment.
20. Keep REMAINING_WORK open until reader, tree, composer, hub, and deployment are proven.

Gevurah does not choke the light; it shapes the glass so the light can be read.
